definition: The person or organisation that owns the insurance contract and pays the premium.
The person or property covered by the policy. Often the policyholder, but not always.
The price paid for cover, usually annually or in instalments.
Deciding whether to accept a risk and on what terms and price.
A characteristic used to price a risk, such as age, location or claims history.
A change to a policy during its term, such as a new address or added cover.
Offering and agreeing cover for a further term.
A policy that ends because the premium was not paid or the customer did not renew.
The first report of a claim, when the basic facts are captured.
An independent expert who investigates and values a claim for the insurer.
Money set aside for claims that have been reported but not yet paid (case reserve) or not yet reported (IBNR).
Incurred but not reported: claims for events that have happened but have not yet been notified.
The insurer's right to recover a claim payment from the party responsible for the loss.
Cover for the cost of legal advice and action, also called legal aid insurance in some markets.
A firm that arranges insurance on behalf of customers and is paid commission or fees.
An arrangement where a coverholder or managing general agent underwrites or settles claims on the insurer's behalf.
A periodic report of policies or claims written under delegated authority.
A price comparison website that collects quotes from several insurers.
Insurance bought by an insurer to transfer part of its risk. Treaty covers a portfolio; facultative covers one risk.
Claims incurred divided by premiums earned.
Loss ratio plus expense ratio. Below 100% means an underwriting profit.
EU prudential framework for insurers: capital requirements (Pillar 1), governance and risk management including ORSA (Pillar 2), and reporting and disclosure (Pillar 3).

Amendments to the Solvency II Directive published in January 2025, applying at the latest from 30 January 2027. Changes cover proportionality, Pillar 1 calibration, macroprudential tools, sustainability risks and reporting.
Solvency capital requirement and minimum capital requirement under Solvency II.
Own risk and solvency assessment: the insurer's own view of its risks and capital needs.
Solvency II reporting: quantitative reporting templates, the public solvency and financial condition report, and the regular supervisory report.
The accounting standard for insurance contracts, effective from January 2023.
EU Insurance Distribution Directive: rules on how insurance is sold, including demands and needs, product oversight and governance, and conflicts of interest.
IDD rules requiring insurers to design, approve and review products for a defined target market.

EU Digital Operational Resilience Act, applying since 17 January 2025. Covers ICT risk management, incident reporting, resilience testing and ICT third-party risk for insurers and other financial entities.
The DORA register of all ICT third-party arrangements that each financial entity must keep and report.
The DORA article listing the key contract terms required for ICT services, such as service descriptions, locations, audit rights and exit.
A function whose disruption would materially impair the insurer's performance, compliance or continuity. Used by DORA and by Solvency II outsourcing rules.
Under Solvency II, outsourcing a critical or important function needs prior notification to the supervisor and stronger contract terms and oversight.

EU regulation on artificial intelligence. AI used for risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance is high-risk. A provisional agreement in 2026 moved stand-alone high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 (to confirm).
